A pattern change is in store for Eastern Kentucky during the long 
term forecast period, and it should bring some relief from the 
recent heat with it. The previously-dominant ridging over the 
Tennessee Valley is progged to retrograde west towards the Ozarks 
this weekend. At the same time, a closed upper level low will move 
over the Floridian Peninsula and set up a Rex-esque blocking feature 
for a few days. Models collectively resolve both of these features 
sitting in place through Sunday morning, although the ridging will 
be in a weakening state. A series of troughing disturbances ejecting 
around the ridge's northern periphery will work in tandem with this 
closed low to suppress the ridge by early next week. While the 
initial two disturbances will yield minor sensible weather impacts 
across the forecast area, a deeper trough is expected to eject out 
of the Rockies early next week. While models disagree on its exact 
evolution, they do agree that it will be the final nail in the 
coffin for the antecedent ridging pattern. Between Friday morning 
and Monday afternoon, the ridge is poised to weaken from its peak 
"heat dome" intensity of 600+ decameters to a looser-organized ridge 
of sub-590 decameter heights. Therefore, this late-period troughing 
disturbance is more likely to bring noticeable heat relief to all of 
Eastern Kentucky than its predecessors.  

The first disturbance is expected to pass well to the north of the 
Ohio River Valley on Friday, with weak northwesterly flow and 
minuscule midlevel height falls modeled across the forecast area. 
While a surface frontal boundary is resolved in the vicinity of the 
forecast area in this time frame, there will be little to no 
syntopic-scale airmass modification associated with it. Temperatures 
in the northeastern half of the CWA will be a few degrees cooler 
than they were in the short term forecast period, but this moreso a 
byproduct of the cloud cover from the convective activity associated 
with the boundary. Given the lack of dynamic support aloft, any 
showers/storms on Friday will be well below severe limits. The lack 
of forcing should also limit the heavy rainfall potential. So, the 
greatest sensible weather effects from this activity will come in 
the form of a SW->NE temperature gradient. There could be a 10 
degree difference in highs on Friday between NE KY and areas west of 
I-75 that are closer to the influence of the ridge. The latest data 
blend accordingly depicts highs in the mid 80s in the Big 
Sandy/Licking River Basin, whereas places closer to the Cumberland 
River will experience yet another day of temperatures in the 90s. 
Any rain that does fall on Friday could help bolster the areal 
coverage of fog on Friday night, when temperatures should cool into 
the 60s area wide.  

Given the blocking to the south and the quasi-zonal flow aloft, the 
boundary responsible for Friday's activity is expected to hang 
around into Saturday. Models resolve low-level flow adopting more of 
a southerly directional component on Saturday and Sunday, this is 
associated with the boundary nudging back north of the Ohio River in 
this time frame. The resultant warm air advection will bump 
temperatures back into the upper 80s/lower 90s area-wide on both 
days. Isolated summertime showers/storms cannot be ruled out during 
peak diurnal heating hours on Saturday, but there could be greater 
convective coverage late Saturday night into Sunday. The second 
ridge-riding impulse is expected to arrive in the latter stages of 
the weekend, with relatively greater shortwave support aloft than 
Friday's. WPC has outlined a Marginal Excessive Rainfall outlook in 
the vicinity of the forecast area for late Saturday night and then 
again on Sunday, but this appears contingent on the evolution of 
upstream activity on Saturday night. A few isolated hydro impacts 
cannot be ruled out where multiple rounds of activity occur in the 
vicinity of the increasingly stationary boundary, but this is 
most likely to be north and northeast of the JKL CWA. 

There is a notable increase in model spread within the NBM ensemble 
across multiple sensible weather forecast parameters for Sunday and 
beyond. This is likely due to differing model solutions 
surrounding the third trough ejecting out of the Rockies. 
Significant variations in this feature's modeled amplitude, 
orientation, phasing, and forward progression speed preclude the 
discussion of specific forecast details at the present moment, but 
models generally agree that a deeper, vertically-stacked trough will 
move through the Midwest and the Greater Ohio River Valley by 
midweek. It would take a trough like this to finally drag a 
meaningful cold front through the CWA, and despite the model spread, 
there is a noticeable downward trend in the mean forecast MaxTs and
